section.title: Glorify God in Your Body
section.sectionRationale: Some in Corinth had turned a slogan of Christian freedom, everything is permissible, into a license for sexual sin, treating the body as morally irrelevant. Paul answers with the highest theology of the body in the New Testament: the body is for the Lord, our bodies are members of Christ, and each believer's body is a temple of the Holy Spirit. Because we were bought at a price, we are not our own, and so the body is a place to glorify God, not to indulge the flesh.
section.thesis: Christian freedom is real but never limitless: the body is not made for immorality but for the Lord, joined to Christ and indwelt by the Spirit, so the redeemed, who are not their own but bought at a price, must flee sexual immorality and glorify God in the body.
section.frameNote: Three movements: freedom weighed and the body claimed for the Lord; union with Christ against union with immorality; the body as the Spirit's temple, bought at a price, made to glorify God.

units.label: Free, but not your own master
units.note: the body is for the Lord

verses.text: “Everything is {{exestin|permissible}} for me,” but not everything is beneficial. “Everything is permissible for me,” but I will not be mastered by anything.
“Food for the stomach and the stomach for food,” but God will destroy them both. The body is not intended for sexual immorality, but for the Lord, and the Lord for the body.
By His power God raised the Lord from the dead, and He will raise us also.

units.label: Members of Christ, not of immorality

verses.text: Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ? Shall I then take the members of Christ and unite them with a prostitute? Never!
Or don’t you know that he who unites himself with a prostitute is one with her in body? For it is said, “The two will become one flesh.”
But he who unites himself with the Lord is one with Him in spirit.
Flee from {{porneia|sexual immorality}}. Every other sin a man can commit is outside his body, but he who sins sexually sins against his own body.

units.label: A temple bought at a price

verses.text: Do you not know that your body is a {{naos|temple}} of the Holy Spirit who is in you, whom you have received from God? You are not your own;
you were {{agorazo|bought}} at a price. Therefore {{doxazo|glorify}} God with your body.

exestin.gloss: It is permitted, it is lawful. Paul quotes a Corinthian slogan celebrating freedom, then qualifies it twice: not everything is beneficial, and he refuses to be mastered by anything. Christian liberty is genuine, but it is measured by love, by what builds up, and by the lordship of Christ, not by mere permission.

porneia.gloss: Sexual immorality of every kind, here especially union with a prostitute. Unlike sins committed outside the body, Paul says this sin is committed against one's own body, which belongs to the Lord and is joined to Christ, so the only faithful response is to flee.

naos.gloss: The inner sanctuary, the holy dwelling place of God, not merely the temple precincts. Paul calls the believer's very body a naos where the Holy Spirit lives. The presence of God once localized in Jerusalem now indwells the redeemed, making holiness of body a matter of worship.

agorazo.gloss: To buy, to purchase in the marketplace, the language of redemption. Believers were bought at a price, the blood of Christ, and so they no longer belong to themselves. Ownership has changed hands; the body is now the Lord's, to be used for His glory.

doxazo.gloss: To glorify, to honor, to make the worth of someone visible. The whole argument drives here: the redeemed body is not a private possession to indulge but an instrument to display the glory of God who made it, raised it, indwells it, and bought it.

basic.context: Some Corinthians were saying everything is permissible and using it to excuse visiting prostitutes, as if the body did not matter to God. Paul answers that the body matters enormously. It is made for the Lord, it will be raised like Christ's, it is joined to Christ, and it is the temple where the Holy Spirit lives. Because Jesus bought us with His own life, we are not our own, so we should run from sexual sin and use our bodies to honor God.
basic.hermeneutics: Paul takes the Corinthians' own slogans, everything is permissible and food for the stomach, and answers them point by point. He is not against freedom; he is against a freedom that ignores who Christ is, what the body is for, and who now owns us. The passage moves from freedom to lordship to redemption, and lands on a command to glorify God in the body.
basic.originalLanguages: The slogan is exestin, it is permitted, which Paul both grants and limits. The sin to flee is porneia, sexual immorality. The believer's body is a naos, the holy inner sanctuary where God dwells. And the reason we are not our own is agorazo, we were bought at a price, so the goal is to doxazo, to glorify God in the body.
basic.typology: The temple, once the house of God in Jerusalem, is fulfilled in Christ and now in His Spirit-indwelt people, whose bodies are living sanctuaries. The redemption language, bought at a price, fulfills the Passover and the ransom of Israel, now accomplished by the blood of Christ.
basic.christ: The body belongs to the Lord Jesus, who was raised bodily and will raise us. Our bodies are members of Christ, so joining them to sin dishonors Him personally. Above all, we were bought at a price: the price is Christ's own blood, and that purchase is why the body is His to glorify.
basic.god: God is not indifferent to the body; He made it, He will raise it, and He gives His Spirit to dwell in it. God is holy, and so His temple must be holy. God is also the great redeemer who paid the highest price to make rebels His own.
basic.crossReferences: Romans 12 calls us to offer our bodies as living sacrifices. 1 Corinthians 3 already called the church God's temple; here it narrows to the individual body. 1 Peter 1 says we were redeemed with the precious blood of Christ. Genesis 2 lies behind the one flesh union Paul cites.
basic.oneStory: The God who made human bodies in the garden, and whose glory once filled the temple, now dwells by His Spirit in the bodies of the redeemed. What sin defiles, Christ has bought back with His blood, so that the body becomes again what it was made to be, a place where God is glorified.

context.literary:
The unit is a dialogue in which one side is heard only through quotation. Verses 12 and 13 contain at least two slogans, 'Everything is permissible for me' and 'Food for the stomach and the stomach for food,' and each is given a 'but' that turns it round. Paul grants the slogan its small truth and then fences it. The BSB marks them with quotation marks, which is an editorial decision, since Greek had none, but it is the reading that best explains how abruptly Paul seems to contradict himself.

The movement is a ladder of three claims about the body, each introduced by a question or an assertion that the Corinthians should already know. The body is for the Lord and will be raised, verses 13 and 14. The body is a member of Christ, verses 15 to 17. The body is the Spirit's sanctuary and has been bought, verses 19 and 20. Verse 18, 'Flee,' is the single imperative in the middle, a hinge between the claims about union and the claims about ownership.

The passage is also tightly paired with the one before it and the one after it. The word 'permissible' of verse 12 returns in 10:23 in the same slogan, where Paul applies it to food offered to idols, and 'bought at a price' returns word for word in 7:23. So 6:20 is not a stray flourish but a refrain Paul uses to frame the whole run of chapters on bodies, marriage and freedom.

The closing 'Therefore glorify God' is short and almost abrupt. After eight verses of argument the one positive command is a single sentence, and the BSB's footnote notes that some later manuscripts add 'and with your spirit, which belong to God,' which is likely a pious expansion.
context.historical:
Corinth sat on a narrow isthmus with a harbour on either side, which made it a place where sailors, merchants and visitors arrived in large numbers, and the city had a reputation for sexual indulgence. Scholars debate how much of that reputation is the exaggeration of rival writers, and how much can be assigned to the cult of Aphrodite, so it is safest to say only that prostitution was common and socially accepted, especially for men, and that dinners in honour of gods often ended in it. The church's members had come out of that world.

The slogans point to a particular kind of religion. Some Greek thought taught that the soul is the true self and the body a temporary shell, so that what happens in the body does not touch the person. A man who believes that will find it easy to say that sex is like eating, a matter of appetite and nothing more, and the Corinthians' denial of the resurrection of the body, 15:12, comes from the same root. If the body is going to be thrown away, why does it matter?

Paul's answer would have startled both Greek and Jewish ears. To a Greek, the idea that the body is raised was foolish. To a Jew, the idea that a body could be a temple was hard to take in, because the temple was a building in Jerusalem where God's glory dwelt, Exodus 40:34-35. For Paul the sanctuary has moved into the people.

The language of purchase also had a social setting. Slaves were bought and sold in markets, and a person who bought a slave owned that person's body and its services. Paul uses that world to say that the believer has a new owner, and that the new owner's rights extend to the body.
context.canonical:
The central text behind verse 16 is Genesis 2:24, 'the two will become one flesh,' which Paul quotes in a form close to the Greek Septuagint, with 'the two.' Jesus quoted the same verse against casual divorce, Matthew 19:5, and Paul will apply it to Christ and the church in Ephesians 5:31-32. Here he does something striking: he reads the verse as a statement about what any sexual union does, not only a married one. A union with a prostitute is not neutral, because the act is the kind of act that makes two into one.

The temple theme runs from the tabernacle, where 'the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle,' Exodus 40:34, through the promise of Ezekiel 37:26-27 that God would set His sanctuary among His people forever. Jesus spoke of the 'temple of His body,' John 2:21, and the apostles then apply the image to the church, 1 Corinthians 3:16, 2 Corinthians 6:16 and Ephesians 2:19-22. Verse 19 narrows that corporate temple down to the individual body without cancelling it.

The language of redemption goes back to the exodus and to the purchase of the firstborn, and it is carried forward in Titus 2:14, 1 Peter 1:18-19, Acts 20:28 and Revelation 5:9. All of these speak of a price that was paid, and all identify it with the blood of Christ.

The command to 'flee' sits next to 10:14, 'flee from idolatry,' and the other bodily commands in Romans 6:12-13 and 12:1, and 1 Thessalonians 4:3-8 shows the same logic applied to holiness and sexual conduct. Taken together, these passages teach that the body is not a lesser part of salvation but the place where its claims are felt.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul is trying to break the link between freedom and indifference. The Corinthians have heard that they are free from the law and have concluded that what the body does does not matter. He replies that real freedom is the freedom of someone who belongs to a good master, and that this master has rights over the body. He wants them to see the body as a participant in redemption, not a detached tool. It is destined for resurrection, it is already joined to Christ, and it is already the dwelling of the Holy Spirit.

He also wants them to feel the weight of the act. A man who goes to a prostitute thinks that he is doing something small and private. Paul asks him to picture it as taking a limb of Christ and joining it to someone else. The shock of the picture is deliberate, and he expects the hearers to recoil with 'Never!'

Finally, he wants a way of life rather than a list of rules. The command to 'flee' is practical, but the closing command, 'glorify God with your body,' is wide open. Paul wants believers to ask what honours God in the body in every setting, from sex to food to rest, and he assumes that people who know whom they belong to will ask it sincerely.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The passage is thick with description of the Corinthians' own habits, and Paul only quotes them in order to correct them. The slogans are not Christian teaching, and treating them as such misreads the text. What is prescriptive is the single verb 'flee,' the question about the members of Christ, and the final 'glorify.' These bind every believer, in every period.

Some applications need care. The idea that the body is a 'temple' is sometimes taken as a basis for rules about diet, exercise or tattoos, but Paul is not talking about those things. He is talking about sexual union and ownership, and it is better to start there. Wider applications of the principle, such as caring for health or refusing to be mastered by food or drink, are fair, but Paul draws them elsewhere, in verse 12 and in Romans 12:1.

The passage also does not say that sexual sin is unforgivable or that those who have sinned sexually are permanently defiled. The Corinthians had come out of that life, as 6:11 reminds them just before this passage. It does say that the believer who sins in this way acts against what he is, and the right response is the one the gospel always asks for: turn, and flee, and rely on the One who bought you.

debates.question: Which parts of verses 12 to 20 are Corinthian slogans and which are Paul's own words?

views.label: Two slogans, 12 and 13a
views.case: The BSB marks 'Everything is permissible for me' and 'Food for the stomach and the stomach for food' as quotations. Paul qualifies each one at once, which is how he handles slogans elsewhere, 10:23. Reading the rest as Paul's own words keeps the passage coherent.

views.label: Three slogans, adding the claim of verse 18
views.case: Some interpreters hear 'Every other sin a man can commit is outside his body' as another Corinthian saying, a claim that sexual sin is the one sin that cannot touch the body, or that the body is untouched by anything. Paul then answers with the opposite, that sexual sin is the sin against the body, and the BSB's wording leaves that reading open.

views.label: A larger Corinthian argument Paul answers point by point
views.case: A few readers think the whole of verses 12 to 13 is a tight Corinthian syllogism: all things are lawful, the body is for appetite as the stomach is for food, and God will destroy both, so what happens in the body is irrelevant. Paul takes it apart one premise at a time.

debates.bearing: The decision affects how one reads verse 18, not the command to flee. On any view Paul teaches that sexual immorality is a distinct offence against the person who is one flesh with another and one Spirit with the Lord.

debates.question: What does Paul mean by 'you were bought at a price,' and to whom was the price paid?

views.label: A marketplace picture of ownership
views.case: The verb comes from the marketplace, and the image is of a slave purchased and now belonging to a new master. Paul does not say that anyone received the price. The point is the cost and the new ownership, with the cross as the price, as Acts 20:28 and Revelation 5:9 suggest.

views.label: A ransom paid to a hostile power or to justice
views.case: Mark 10:45 speaks of a 'ransom for many,' and some in the church's history have asked who held the captives, whether sin, the devil, or God's own justice. The older answers differ, and the text of 1 Corinthians 6 does not pursue the question.

debates.bearing: The passage presses on the believer the fact of the purchase and its cost, and leaves aside questions about the payee. What matters for Paul is that the body now belongs to Christ.

debates.question: In what sense is sexual sin a sin against one's own body, unlike other sins?

views.label: A unique bodily and covenantal union
views.case: Sexual union creates a one flesh bond, so immorality violates the body in a way other sins do not, joining what belongs to Christ to sin itself.

views.label: A slogan Paul is qualifying
views.case: Some read the phrase as another Corinthian saying Paul answers; yet the flow best reads it as Paul's own point about the singular bodily nature of this sin.

debates.bearing: Either reading upholds Paul's command to flee; the mainstream reading stresses that immorality uniquely defiles the body that is joined to Christ and indwelt by the Spirit.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 12 turns on a pair of words from the same root. 'Permissible' is exestin, from exousia, authority or right, and Paul's reply, 'I will not be mastered by anything,' uses the verb exousiazo, to be under someone's authority. The freedom claimed in the slogan is answered in the same family of words: the person who says 'I have the right' can become the one who is ruled. In 7:4 Paul uses the verb of husband and wife, who have 'authority' over one another's bodies, which shows how deliberately he uses it.

In verse 13 the word for 'destroy' is katargeo, which means to render inoperative or bring to an end. Paul uses it of rulers who are passing away, 2:6, and of death, 'the last enemy to be destroyed,' 15:26. The stomach and food belong to an age that is ending, and the body, by contrast, will be raised. Verse 14 changes the verb as well: God 'raised' the Lord, and 'will raise us,' with a compound that stresses the lifting out of the grave.

Verses 16 and 17 depend on kollao, to glue or join, the word that the Septuagint uses in Genesis 2:24 in its compounded form for a man being united to his wife. The same verb describes both unions: the man who is joined to a prostitute and the man who is joined to the Lord. The first makes 'one body,' the second 'one spirit.' Paul is not saying the believer loses his own personality. He is saying that union with Christ is a real union.

The command in verse 18, pheugo, 'flee,' is the same verb he uses for idolatry in 10:14. Paul does not tell the Corinthians to fight or reason with these two sins but to run. The BSB's 'sins against his own body' translates eis, 'against' or 'into,' with a reflexive adjective. The preposition contrasts with 'outside the body,' so the sin is described as an act that goes into the person.

Verse 19 has 'your' in the plural and 'body' in the singular, a distributive singular that means each person's body, though the singular also lets Paul keep the thought of 3:16, where the church together is the temple. Both are true. The word naos is the sanctuary itself, the inner house, and not the whole temple complex, and it is the word John 2:21 uses for Jesus' body.

Finally, in verse 20 the word for 'price' is time, which also means honour. Paul probably does not intend the pun, but it is true that the one who paid the price now has the right to be honoured with the body.

typology.type: The tabernacle filled with glory, Exodus 40:34-35
typology.fulfillment: When the tabernacle was finished, a cloud covered the tent and 'the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle,' so much that Moses could not enter. The sanctuary was holy because God's presence made it so, and the whole camp was arranged around it. Paul applies this to the believer's body: the Spirit now lives in it, Romans 8:11, and so it is the place of God's presence. The escalation is from one building to every believer, and from a tent that could be moved to a body that goes everywhere. The type is imperfect because the tabernacle could be entered only by priests; the body is a sanctuary by grace to every believer.

typology.type: The firstborn redeemed and Israel brought out, Isaiah 43:1
typology.fulfillment: The Lord says to Israel, 'I have redeemed you; I have called you by your name; you are Mine!' The exodus was the great purchase of a people from slavery, and from then on Israel belonged to the Lord. Paul's 'you are not your own' says the same of the church, now redeemed by the blood of Christ, 1 Peter 1:18-19. The correspondence deepens because the price is no longer a lamb but the Lamb, and the people redeemed are no longer one nation but those from every tribe and tongue, Revelation 5:9. The type falls short in that Israel's redemption was from Egypt and the church's from sin and death.

Genesis presents marriage as a union in which two become one. Paul reads the verse as describing the weight of any sexual union and then sets beside it a greater union, 'one with Him in spirit,' verse 17. In Ephesians 5:31-32 he quotes the same verse and says, 'I am speaking about Christ and the church.' The marriage union is therefore a signpost to the union of Christ and His people, which is deeper than the physical and cannot be broken. The type falls short because earthly marriage ends at death, Romans 7:2-3, while union with Christ does not.

typology.type: The body of Christ as the true temple, John 2:19-21
typology.fulfillment: Jesus said, 'Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up again,' and John explains, 'Jesus was speaking about the temple of His body.' The temple pointed ahead to a person in whom God's presence dwelt bodily. The Corinthians, who are joined to Him and indwelt by His Spirit, share in that fulfilment, and Ephesians 2:21-22 speaks of a holy temple built in Him. The correspondence is therefore not that each body is a building but that each is joined to the true temple. The type falls short only in the sense that believers are temples by participation, not by nature.

study.christ:
The passage leads to Christ most directly by the claim that bodies are 'members of Christ,' verse 15. The body of the believer is not simply a vessel for the Spirit; it belongs to the body of the risen Lord, which is the centre of Paul's gospel. Verse 14 anchors that claim in the resurrection. 'By His power God raised the Lord from the dead, and He will raise us also.' The Lord's body is the first part of a harvest that includes ours, 15:20, and that is why what we do with ours matters to Him. The resurrection is also the answer to the Corinthians' slogan. If God did not discard the body of Jesus, He does not discard ours.

It leads to Christ by the price. Paul does not say here what the price was, but he says it elsewhere. The church of God was purchased 'with His own blood,' Acts 20:28, and believers were redeemed 'with the precious blood of Christ,' 1 Peter 1:19. The cost explains the claim. A person who paid so dearly does not hold a loose title to the thing bought. When Paul says 'you are not your own,' he is speaking as one who has seen the cross and knows what was paid.

It leads to Christ by pattern. Jesus, the true temple, could say that His body would be destroyed and raised, John 2:19. He is the one who lived a whole human life in a body without being mastered by anything, and who gave that body up, 'This is My body, which is for you,' 11:24. The believer's bodily holiness is therefore not a rule drawn from nowhere but a sharing in the way Christ used His own body.

It leads to Christ by union. Verse 17 puts it in a few words: 'he who unites himself with the Lord is one with Him in spirit.' The union is not metaphorical, and it is why the sin of verse 15 is so grave: it takes what is joined to Christ and joins it to another. Romans 8:11 adds that the Spirit who raised Jesus lives in believers and will 'give life to your mortal bodies.' What Christ is, the believer shares.

A caution keeps the reading honest. Paul does not say that believers become Christ or that the body is divine. He says the body is Christ's, and it is for Him. The union is real but not an identity, and the right response is gratitude and obedience, not pride.
study.god:
The passage shows a God who is not embarrassed by the body. He made it, He will raise it, and He chooses to live in it. This is a surprising thing to say in a world that has often treated the physical as a lower and lesser part of religion. In verse 13, 'the body ... for the Lord, and the Lord for the body,' the Lord is not an idea to be contemplated apart from the flesh but a person who has a body Himself, and the believer's body is the place where he is honoured. The God of this passage is the God of the incarnation, and so He takes seriously what we do with our bodies.

It also shows a God who owns what He has bought. Ownership in Scripture is not tyranny. Israel was told, 'you are Mine,' Isaiah 43:1, in a verse that begins with 'Do not fear.' The same God who says 'you are not your own' also says that He will not let go. His ownership is the ground of protection, and the one who has been bought by Him does not need to serve the appetites that used to rule him. Verse 12 says that those who are not mastered by anything are those who have a master.

The passage is also trinitarian. The Father raised the Lord by His power, the Lord has members who are His body, and the Holy Spirit lives in the body 'whom you have received from God.' Paul speaks of all three in the course of a single argument about sexual conduct. The doctrine of God is not an abstract topic here; it is the reason a man should not go to a prostitute.

The God of this passage is holy. He does not share His dwelling with sin, and Paul assumes that the Corinthians know it from the temple. The same holiness is the reason He is also merciful. He does not leave a defiled people in their defilement but washes and sanctifies them, as verse 11 told the Corinthians, and then lives in them.

For worship this means that the body is brought into praise. 'Glorify God with your body' is a call to worship that is lived in the whole person, and Romans 12:1 calls it 'your spiritual service of worship.' We worship a God who has bought us, who is present in us, and who will raise us, so every use of the body, from prayer to rest to marriage to refusal, can be done for His glory.

crossReferences.note: The verse Paul quotes in verse 16. A man is united to his wife and the two become one flesh. Paul reads it as describing what sexual union does, so that even an act with a prostitute joins two people in a way that cannot be treated as trivial.

Paul repeats the slogan about what is permissible, again with the answer that not everything is beneficial or builds up. The pair of texts shows that he used the same pattern of grant and limit whenever a Corinthian claimed freedom as a reason to do what harmed others or themselves.

'You were bought at a price; do not become slaves of men.' Paul repeats the line from 6:20 in the next chapter, applying it to social status and obedience. The purchase explains both the body's holiness here and a believer's freedom from human masters there.

Some in Corinth said there is no resurrection of the dead. That denial is the likely root of the idea that the body does not matter. Paul's insistence in 6:14 that God will raise us answers it in advance, and chapter 15 then argues the case in full.

Paul uses the same verb for idolatry that he uses for sexual immorality: flee. The two are linked throughout the letter, and in both cases the right response to a deep temptation is to run from it, not to test how close one can stand.

Jesus speaks of 'the temple of His body,' using the word for the inner sanctuary. The link shows why Paul can call a believer's body a temple. It belongs to the one who is the true temple, and it shares in his resurrection life.

Paul tells the Romans not to let sin reign in the mortal body and not to present the parts of the body as instruments of wickedness, but as instruments of righteousness. It carries the same idea as 1 Corinthians 6: the body is a place of service, and it is to be presented to God.

The believer is told to offer the body as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God, as spiritual worship. This gives a positive picture of what 'glorify God with your body' means. The body is not only to be kept from wrongdoing but to be given as an offering.

The readers were redeemed not with perishable things like silver or gold but with the precious blood of Christ. The text states plainly what 1 Corinthians 6:20 leaves unsaid, which is what the price was and why it makes the body holy.

The church of God is described as the flock 'which He purchased with His own blood.' The language of purchase is used of the whole church, and the phrase 'His own blood' shows the cost. Paul's 'bought at a price' in 1 Corinthians has the same source and weight.

The church is described as a holy temple in the Lord, built on the apostles and prophets with Christ as the cornerstone, and as a dwelling for God in His Spirit. It carries the corporate side of the temple image that 1 Corinthians 3:16 uses and that 6:19 narrows to the individual.

It is God's will that you be holy, abstaining from sexual immorality and controlling the body in holiness and honour, and God has not called believers to impurity. The passage is a close parallel to 1 Corinthians 6 and confirms that Paul taught this consistently across his churches.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with a God who makes a body from the dust and breathes into it, and calls the whole creation, bodies included, 'very good,' Genesis 1:31. The first humans were placed in a garden that was also a kind of sanctuary, where God walked with them, and their bodies were the place where they carried His image. The fall did not abolish the body, but it made it a place of shame, hiding and death, Genesis 3:7-19. The story that follows is the story of God working to restore what was broken, and it is the story of a body being redeemed.

The question this passage answers is whether salvation is only about souls. Paul says no. The same God who raised Jesus will raise us, and meanwhile He has chosen to live in us. The tabernacle and the temple were stages in a long process of making a dwelling for God among His people, and with the coming of the Spirit that process moves to its next stage: He lives in human beings. The garden, the tent, the house in Jerusalem, the body of Jesus, the church and now the individual believer are all links in a chain that runs through the Bible.

The passage also sets up the end of the story. If the body is destined for resurrection, then the new creation is not a spiritual escape but a physical renewal, and the Bible's last chapters describe a city, a river and a tree, Revelation 22:1-2. In that city God's presence is not confined to a building, because 'the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple,' Revelation 21:22, and His servants 'will see His face,' Revelation 22:4.

Between the garden and the city, believers live in bodies that are still subject to weakness and temptation, which is why Paul gives a command and not only a promise. The call to flee and to glorify God is the way a redeemed person lives in the period between promise and fulfilment. A body that is a temple of the Holy Spirit already belongs to the new creation, and the way it is used is a small preview of the world to come.

quiz.q: How does Paul respond to the slogan everything is permissible?

options.text: He grants a measure of freedom but limits it: not everything is beneficial, and he will not be mastered.
options.note: Paul qualifies the slogan by benefit and by refusing to be enslaved to anything.

options.text: He fully endorses it as the heart of Christian liberty.
options.note: He immediately qualifies it; unlimited license is exactly what he corrects.

options.text: He says it applies only to food, never to the body.
options.note: He does distinguish food from the body, but his main point is that freedom is bounded by lordship.

options.text: He rejects all Christian freedom outright.
options.note: Paul affirms real freedom; he simply denies that it excuses sin.

quiz.q: Why does Paul say the body is not for sexual immorality?

options.text: Because the body is for the Lord, joined to Christ as His member.
options.note: The body belongs to the Lord and is a member of Christ, so it cannot be given to immorality.

options.text: Because the body is unimportant and will be discarded.
options.note: The opposite is true; God will raise the body, so it matters eternally.

options.text: Because sexual desire is inherently sinful.
options.note: Paul does not condemn the body or desire itself, but immorality that dishonors the Lord.

options.text: Because marriage is the only proper use of the body.
options.note: True as far as it goes, but Paul's stated reason is that the body is for the Lord.

quiz.q: What does Paul mean by calling the body a temple of the Holy Spirit?

options.text: The Spirit dwells in the believer's body, making it a holy sanctuary for God.
options.note: The naos is God's dwelling; the Spirit indwells the believer, so the body is holy.

options.text: The body is a building we visit for worship.
options.note: The point is the reverse; the body itself is the dwelling, not a place we go.

options.text: Only the gathered church, not the individual, is God's temple.
options.note: The church is God's temple elsewhere, but here Paul speaks of the individual body.

options.text: The Spirit visits occasionally but does not dwell.
options.note: Paul says the Spirit is in you, a settled indwelling, not an occasional visit.

quiz.q: What is the ground of Paul's command to glorify God in the body?

options.text: You are not your own; you were bought at a price.
options.note: Redemption changes ownership: the body now belongs to the Lord who bought it.

options.text: You must earn your salvation by bodily discipline.
options.note: The logic is the reverse; because we are already bought, we glorify God.

options.text: Your body is your own to do with as you please.
options.note: Paul says precisely the opposite: you are not your own.

options.text: The body should be honored because it is naturally good.
options.note: The body is good, but Paul's stated ground is that we were bought at a price.

quiz.q: What price is behind the phrase bought at a price?

options.text: The blood of Christ, who redeemed us for God.
options.note: Redemption language points to the ransom paid in Christ's own blood.

options.text: Our own good works offered to God.
options.note: The price is Christ's, not ours; we are the ones purchased.

options.text: A general debt that remains unpaid.
options.note: The price has been fully paid, decisively, by Christ.

options.text: The cost of temple sacrifices we still must bring.
options.note: The old sacrifices pointed forward, but the price paid is Christ's blood, once for all.

questions: Everything is permissible, but not everything is beneficial. Where might you be using freedom in a way that is technically allowed but not truly good for you or others?
Paul says he will not be mastered by anything. What habit or appetite is quietly mastering you, and what would it look like to be free of it under Christ?
Your body is a member of Christ and a temple of the Holy Spirit. How does knowing that God dwells in you change the way you treat your body?
Paul's command is simply to flee sexual immorality. What practical steps of fleeing, not just resisting, do you need to take?
You are not your own; you were bought at a price. How would living as someone who belongs to Christ reshape your choices this week?

translationNotes.note: Everything is permissible for me appears in quotation marks because Paul is citing a Corinthian slogan and then qualifying it; the phrase is theirs, the correction is his.
Temple renders naos, the inner sanctuary or holy dwelling place, not the whole temple complex, stressing that the body is the very place where God's Spirit dwells.
Bought at a price uses the marketplace verb for purchase, the language of redemption; the price, unstated here, is the blood of Christ, and the result is that the body now belongs to God.
